metaDescription: Four Keystone dehumidifiers from 22 to 50 pints compared by pump, wheels and coverage so you can match one to a bedroom, basement or large open room.
expertTake: The Keystone 50-pint with the built-in pump is the pick for a basement without a floor drain, and the 35-pint is the value pick for a bedroom or mid-size room. If you only need to dry a closet or a bathroom corner, skip this compressor range and use a small desiccant unit.
introParagraphs: A family of basic dehumidifiers earns its keep through three plain traits: a capacity that fits the room, a drain that suits the house and controls that a tired owner can actually use. Fancy extras matter far less than getting those three right.
A narrow lineup makes the choice easier because there are only a few steps to compare. The work is in matching the step to the space, then deciding whether the drain needs a pump.

products.name: Keystone 50-Pint Dehumidifier with Built-In Pump, 4,500 Sq Ft

specList.label: Best space
specList.value: Large basement without a floor drain

products.description:
The pump model is the one that solves the most real problems. A built-in pump lifts condensate through a hose to a sink or a standpipe, so a basement without a floor drain on the same level becomes workable. Most compressor units at this size rely entirely on gravity, which is why the pump earns its place in a lineup of four.

Its 50-pint rating and 4,500 square foot coverage match the plain 50-pint Keystone, and the settings include normal, turbo and auto-defrost modes. Turbo pushes the fan harder for a fast pull-down after a wet spell, while auto-defrost clears coil frost in a cool room. The step up from the 35-pint is fifteen pints of capacity, which is the margin that matters in a damp open space.

Ownership centers on the hose and the filter. Keep the discharge line free of kinks, rinse the filter every few weeks and test the pump when the humid season starts. A pump hides how much water the machine is removing, so glance at the discharge now and then to confirm it is still flowing.
products.bestFor: Large basements where the drain is above the machine.
pros: Built-in pump lifts water to a distant drain
Turbo and auto-defrost modes for different conditions
50-pint capacity for rooms up to 4,500 square feet
Fifteen more pints than the 35-pint model
cons: Pump is a part that needs a seasonal test

products.name: Keystone 50-Pint Dehumidifier with LED Display, 4,500 Sq Ft
products.description:
The LED display model keeps the same 50-pint class and 4,500 square foot rating but leaves out the pump. It is the better pick when the basement has a floor drain at or below the machine's level, because a gravity hose does the same work with one fewer part. The LED panel makes the setpoint and the current humidity easy to read at a glance.

The four caster wheels are a quiet strength. A 50-pint machine is heavy enough that most owners avoid moving it, and wheels remove that excuse, so it is easier to pull the unit out to clean the coil or to move it between a basement and a garage. The listing also describes quiet operation, which helps if the machine sits near a finished area.

The tradeoff is flexibility. Without a pump the drain must run downhill, and the bucket fills quickly at 50 pints in a wet room, so a hose is the practical setup. Keep the intake clear of the wall and wash the filter regularly.
products.bestFor: Basements with a floor drain that need 50-pint capacity.
pros: LED display shows setpoint and humidity clearly
Four caster wheels make moving it easy
50-pint capacity at a lower cost than the pump model
Quiet operation noted in the listing
cons: No pump, so the drain must be downhill
Bucket fills quickly in a wet room

products.name: Keystone 35-Pint Dehumidifier, Up to 3,000 Sq Ft
products.description:
The 35-pint is the middle step: more output than the 22-pint and less bulk than the 50-pint models. With coverage listed up to 3,000 square feet, it can handle a bedroom, a bathroom or a mid-size basement where the problem is steady but not severe. The listing mentions normal, turbo and auto-defrost settings, the same as the larger units.

Its size is the selling point. The cabinet is smaller and lighter than the 50-pint models, so it is easier to carry and tuck beside a bed or into a utility corner. The listing also notes quiet operation, which fits a bedroom use.

It will struggle in a wet unfinished basement, where a 50-pint is the right tool. In a mid-size room it is an economical choice, and a hose keeps it running when you cannot empty the bucket daily. Wash the filter monthly and keep the room closed to limit the air volume the unit has to treat.
products.bestFor: Bedrooms and mid-size rooms with a steady humidity problem.
pros: Smaller and lighter than the 50-pint models
Marketed as quiet enough for a bedroom
cons: Not enough for a wet unfinished basement
Bucket fills sooner than the 50-pint models

products.name: Keystone Energy Star 22-Pint Portable Dehumidifier, 1,500 Sq Ft
products.description:
The 22-pint is the smallest Keystone and the only one here that lists Energy Star certification. It is rated for up to 1,500 square feet, which fits a bedroom, a bathroom or a small utility room. Auto-shutoff stops the unit when the bucket is full, and a timer lets you run it on a schedule.

Measured at the federal test of 65F and 60% RH, a 22-pint rating is stronger than it sounds. Older labels used a warmer condition, so a modern 22 pint unit is roughly equal to an old 30 pint unit. Even so, it has less coil and a smaller bucket than the 35-pint, so it is a poor choice for a damp basement.

It is the easiest to carry and store. Use it in a closed room, empty the bucket when the shutoff trips and clean the filter monthly. If you are choosing between this and the 35-pint for a bedroom, the Energy Star badge and the lower running cost favor the smaller unit when the room is genuinely small.
products.bestFor: Single bedrooms and bathrooms where efficiency matters.
pros: Energy Star certified for lower running cost
cons: Only 1,500 square feet of listed coverage
Too small for a damp basement

buyingCriteria.explanation: Keystone offers 22, 35 and 50 pint steps, rated for roughly 1,500, 3,000 and 4,500 square feet. A bedroom or bathroom suits the 22-pint, a mid-size room suits the 35-pint and a basement suits a 50-pint. If the space smells musty or has visible condensation, go one step up from what the floor area suggests. The coverage label assumes open floor and a mild problem, so a basement divided into rooms by closed doors behaves like several small spaces, and a single unit placed in one room will do little for the others.

The 50-pint with pump lifts water to a distant drain, while the plain 50-pint with the LED display relies on gravity. A pump matters only when the drain is above the machine or on another level. If a floor drain sits within reach, the cheaper plain model does the same work with fewer parts. Measure the vertical rise from the machine to the discharge point before ordering, and remember that a long horizontal run can reduce how high a small pump can push the water.

The 50-pint with LED display has four caster wheels, which makes it far easier to move for cleaning. The 35-pint and 22-pint are lighter and easier to carry. A machine you cannot move is a machine whose coil never gets cleaned. Wheels also help when you rotate the unit between a basement in summer and a damp garage or laundry room in spring, which stretches the value of a single purchase across more rooms.

A compressor unit loses output when the coil frosts below about 65F. The 35-pint and 50-pint models list auto-defrost, which clears frost and keeps the unit working. In a basement that sits near 60F, that mode is worth having. Even with defrost, expect output below the label figure in a cold room, so a space that hovers near 55F will need a larger unit or a gentle source of heat to reach the same result.

The LED panel on the plain 50-pint shows the setpoint and the current humidity clearly. The 22-pint adds a timer and auto-shutoff. Pick the layout you will actually read, because a hard-to-read control invites guessing. A readout of current humidity also lets you see whether the unit is making progress, which is the fastest way to learn if the room is too big for it.

A unit that runs for months pays its electric bill many times over. The 22-pint lists Energy Star certification, which signals lower consumption per pint. For bigger units, sizing correctly matters more than any badge, since a machine that cycles off uses less power than one running flat out. Over a humid summer the difference between a right-sized machine and one that never reaches its setpoint can add up to a noticeable amount on the electric bill.

howWeEvaluated.title: Capacity ladder
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared the 22, 35 and 50 pint steps and their listed coverage of 1,500, 3,000 and 4,500 square feet. The spread between steps makes it simple to match a unit to a room. We treated the figures as spec sheet claims, not measurements. We also asked whether each step is large enough to matter, since fifteen pints separates the 35-pint from the 50-pint models and that gap decides whether a damp room ever reaches its setpoint.

howWeEvaluated.title: Drain options
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at the pump on one 50-pint model and the gravity drain on the others. Where the drain sits high or far away, the pump model came out ahead. A hose port scored well for simple use. We also gave credit to models that offer both a bucket and a hose, since that lets an owner start simple and change later.

howWeEvaluated.title: Handling and controls
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed the four casters and LED display on the plain 50-pint against the lighter smaller models. Easy movement and readable controls matter in year-three ownership. A machine that is awkward to pull out tends to skip its yearly coil cleaning, which shows up as slower drying after a couple of seasons.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cool-room features
howWeEvaluated.description: We noted auto-defrost and turbo modes on the 35 and 50 pint models. Cool basements are a common failure case for compressor units. A model with no stated cool-room feature scored lower for an unheated space, because frost on the coil is the quiet way a unit stops working.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value and efficiency
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared relative price tiers, from the 22-pint at a lower tier to the pump model at the top. We also noted the Energy Star label on the 22-pint. For value, pick the smallest Keystone that copes with the room.

cards.label: Pump (50-Pint with Pump)
cards.text: Lifts water to a distant drain. It suits basements with no floor drain. The pump adds a part that needs an annual check.

cards.label: Gravity or bucket (50-Pint LED, 35-Pint, 22-Pint)
cards.text: Simpler and cheaper with nothing to fail. It needs a downhill path or manual emptying. It suits spaces with a floor drain.

howToChoose.note: Choose the pump when the drain is uphill, and gravity when a floor drain is close.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: At least 50 pints for a moderately damp basement, a drain that works with gravity or a pump and auto-defrost for cool rooms. Place it with clearance around the intake.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The 50-Pint with Pump suits awkward drains, the 50-Pint LED Display is the value choice with a floor drain and the 35-Pint suits a smaller basement.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: The drain is uphill or you want the unit to run unattended. The 50-Pint with Pump earns its cost.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: The room is a bedroom or bathroom. The 22-Pint or 35-Pint handle it for less.

maintenance.why: A clogged filter chokes airflow and invites coil frost. Let the filter dry completely before it goes back in.
Standing water grows slime and odor, and that smell ends up in the room air. Mild soap and a rinse prevent it, and letting the bucket dry before you refit it keeps the film from returning.
A pump that sits idle through a dry winter can stick or lose its prime. Run a cycle with the bucket slightly full and watch the discharge until the flow is steady.

Dust cuts heat transfer and efficiency, and a coil packed with lint is the most common reason a unit slows down in its third summer. Unplug the unit before opening, and use a soft brush and a vacuum with a crevice tool.

Kinks and sediment stop flow and cause overflow, which is how a quiet unit turns into a wet floor. Confirm it drains freely by pouring a cup of water through the line, and replace a hose that has gone stiff or cloudy.

faq.q: Which Keystone size do I need?
faq.a: A bedroom or bathroom suits the 22-pint, a mid-size room suits the 35-pint and a basement suits a 50-pint. If the space smells musty or shows condensation, go one step up so the unit cycles off instead of running constantly.

faq.q: Is the pump model worth it?
faq.a: Yes when the drain is above the machine or on another level. With a floor drain nearby, the plain 50-pint is simpler and avoids a part that can fail. If you plan to leave it running while you are away, either setup works as long as the water has somewhere to go, because a full bucket shuts the unit off. Check the discharge before a long trip and make sure the hose end is secured so it cannot lift out of the drain and spill.

faq.q: Do these work in a cool basement?
faq.a: They list auto-defrost, which clears coil frost in a cool room. Compressor units still lose output below about 65F, so size up a step if the space stays cold.

faq.q: How long should a Keystone last?
faq.a: Compressor dehumidifiers commonly last 5 to 10 years, and the hot compressor of a cheap unit working in humid air is the usual first part to fail. Washing the filter, cleaning the coil and avoiding an undersized unit are the main levers.

faq.q: What does Energy Star mean here?
faq.a: It indicates lower energy use per pint removed. The 22-pint carries it, which helps on a unit that may run for months.

Between 40 and 50 percent is the usual goal. Above 60 percent invites mold, and below 30 percent feels dry. Confirm with a separate hygrometer. Built-in sensors can read a few points off, and a cheap standalone meter in the far corner shows whether the whole room is dry or only the air near the unit.
